subject: Rotorcraft Aerodynamics - Ground Resonance
learning_objective: State the mechanism that develops ground resonance.
question_text: Ground resonance is most likely to develop when

choices.label: A
choices.text: on the ground and harmonic vibrations develop between the main and tail rotors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a series of shocks causes the rotor system to become unbalanced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: there is a combination of a decrease in the angle of attack on the advancing blade and an increase in the angle of attack on the retreating blade.

explanation: Ground resonance develops when a series of shocks (such as a hard or uneven landing) displaces the main rotor blades from their normal, evenly-spaced positions, unbalancing the rotor system and setting up a self-reinforcing vibration that couples with the airframe's natural frequency while in ground contact.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Ground resonance is a main-rotor blade-spacing imbalance phenomenon, not an interaction between main and tail rotors.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This describes dissymmetry-of-lift/blade-flapping behaviour relevant to forward flight and retreating-blade stall, not ground resonance.

subject: Rotorcraft Aerodynamics - Settling with Power
learning_objective: State the hazard associated with a near-vertical, low-airspeed power approach into a confined area.
question_text: If the pilot were to make a near-vertical power approach into a confined area with the airspeed near zero, what hazardous condition may develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ground resonance when ground contact is made.

explanation: A steep, near-vertical, low-airspeed power approach risks the helicopter descending into its own main rotor downwash (settling with power / vortex ring state), causing an increased rate of descent that power alone may not arrest.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Ground resonance is a ground-contact phenomenon related to rotor blade spacing imbalance, not the hazard of a steep low-speed power approach in the air.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 'Blade stall vibration' is not the standard term for this specific hazard; settling with power / vortex ring state is.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-21 (Helicopter Flying Handbook), settling with power.

subject: Rotorcraft Aerodynamics - Dissymmetry of Lift
question_text: The lift differential that exists between the advancing main rotor blade and the retreating main rotor blade is known as
explanation: Dissymmetry of lift is the difference in lift between the advancing blade (higher relative airspeed, more lift) and the retreating blade (lower relative airspeed, less lift) during forward flight.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Transverse flow effect relates to differing airflow over the front and rear of the rotor disk, a related but distinct phenomenon.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hunting tendency refers to a rotor blade's lead/lag motion about its vertical hinge, not the advancing/retreating lift differential.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-21 (Helicopter Flying Handbook), aerodynamics of flight.

subject: Rotorcraft Aerodynamics - Four Forces
learning_objective: List the four forces acting on a helicopter in flight.
question_text: The four forces acting on a helicopter in flight are
explanation: The four fundamental forces acting on a helicopter in flight are lift, drag, thrust, and weight — the same four forces as any other aircraft, though generated and balanced differently by the rotor system.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Weight and gravity are the same force described twice; this option is not a correct independent list of four distinct forces.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Power and friction are not among the standard four aerodynamic forces of flight.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-21 (Helicopter Flying Handbook), aerodynamics of flight.

subject: Emergency Procedures - Engine Failure at Altitude
learning_objective: State the immediate pilot action for an engine failure at altitude in a helicopter.
question_text: What action should the pilot take if engine failure occurs at altitude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Open the throttle as the collective pitch is raised.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduce cyclic back stick pressure during turns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the collective pitch control, as necessary, to maintain rotor RPM.

explanation: Following an engine failure, the pilot must lower the collective pitch control as necessary to maintain rotor RPM and enter autorotation, since rotor RPM decay is the immediate life-critical concern.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Opening the throttle and raising collective assumes engine power is available, which contradicts the engine-failure scenario.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Cyclic back-pressure management during turns is not the primary, immediate action required after an engine failure.

subject: Weather - Fronts
learning_objective: State the one weather change that always occurs when flying across a front.
question_text: One weather phenomenon which will always occur when flying across a front is a change in the
explanation: By definition, a front separates two air masses with different characteristics; a change in wind direction across the boundary is the one feature that is always present, whereas precipitation type and stability change are not guaranteed for every frontal crossing.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Air mass stability may or may not change noticeably across every front.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Precipitation type does not necessarily change across every front (some frontal crossings involve no precipitation at all).

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), meteorology.

subject: Airport Operations - Helicopter Traffic Pattern
learning_objective: State the recommended practice for a helicopter approaching an airport for landing.
question_text: Which is appropriate for a helicopter approaching an airport for landing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remain below the airplane traffic pattern altitude.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Avoid the flow of fixed-wing traffic.

explanation: Helicopter pilots are encouraged to avoid the flow of fixed-wing traffic, since helicopters can safely operate at different patterns, altitudes, and approach paths than airplanes, reducing conflict.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Remaining below airplane pattern altitude is not the specific recommended technique; avoiding the fixed-wing flow generally is the broader guidance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Flying right-hand traffic is not a universal helicopter-specific rule; standard traffic pattern direction depends on the airport, and helicopters are not automatically assigned right traffic.

subject: Airport Operations - VASI
learning_objective: State the approach/landing objective assured by remaining on the VASI glidepath.
question_text: Which approach and landing objective is assured when the pilot remains on the proper glidepath of the VASI?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Safe obstruction clearance in the approach area.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lateral course guidance to the runway.

explanation: A VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator) primarily assures safe obstruction clearance in the approach area as long as the pilot remains on the indicated glidepath; it does not provide lateral/course guidance, which comes from the runway alignment itself.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: VASI is a vertical glidepath aid, not a runway-identification or course-guidance system.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: VASI provides vertical (glidepath), not lateral, guidance.

subject: Performance - Density Altitude
learning_objective: Determine the change in density altitude resulting from a temperature increase at a constant pressure altitude.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 8.) What is the effect of a temperature increase from 35 to 50°F on the density altitude if the pressure altitude remains at 3,000 feet MSL?
explanation: Reading the Density Altitude Chart (Figure 8) at 3,000 ft pressure altitude, density altitude increases by approximately 1,000 feet as temperature rises from 35°F to 50°F, since warmer air is less dense.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Density altitude increases (not decreases) with a temperature rise.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 1,300 feet overstates the increase shown on the chart/by calculation for this specific temperature change.

handbook_reference: FAA-CT-8080-2H, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement, Figure 8 (Density Altitude Chart).
calculation_steps: Using the density-altitude approximation (ISA deviation x ~120 ft/degC): ISA temp at 3,000 ft = 15 - (2x3) = 9 degC. At 35 degF (1.7 degC): deviation = 1.7-9 = -7.3 degC, DA = 3000 + 120x(-7.3) = ~2,120 ft. At 50 degF (10 degC): deviation = 10-9 = 1 degC, DA = 3000 + 120x1 = ~3,120 ft. Difference = ~1,000 ft increase, matching the chart reading and answer key.

subject: Accident/Incident Reporting
learning_objective: State the NTSB written accident report filing deadline.
question_text: The pilot of an aircraft that has been involved in an accident is required to file an NTSB accident report within how many days?
explanation: Following a reportable accident, the operator must file a written report with the NTSB within 10 days (this written-report deadline is separate from the immediate-notification requirement for accidents and certain serious incidents).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 5 days is not the regulatory filing deadline.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 7 days is not the regulatory filing deadline.

subject: Aircraft Systems - Airspeed Indicator Markings
learning_objective: Identify the never-exceed speed marking on an airspeed indicator.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 4.) Which marking identifies the never-exceed speed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upper limit of the green arc.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Upper limit of the white arc.

explanation: The red radial line on an airspeed indicator marks never-exceed speed (Vne), the speed that must never be deliberately exceeded, confirmed on the referenced Figure 4 (Airspeed Indicator) diagram from the FAA-CT-8080-2H supplement.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The upper limit of the green arc is maximum structural cruising speed (Vno), not Vne.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The upper limit of the white arc is maximum flap extension speed (Vfe), not Vne.

handbook_reference: FAA-CT-8080-2H, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement, Figure 4 (Airspeed Indicator).
